439	\subsection{Integrated-moment cubic remainder}\label{sec:momentremainder}
440	The earlier $K_{3i}$ uses the maximum spatial radius everywhere. A sharper scalar-estimator bound integrates known Fourier columns over the cube. Put
441	\begin{equation}
442	c_2=12^{-1/2},\quad c_4=(3/12^2)^{1/4},\quad c_6=(15/12^3)^{1/6}.
443	\end{equation}
444	For any $v\in\R^3$, $\norm{v^\top x}_{L^p(D)}\le c_p\norm{v}$ for $p=2,4,6$. To see this, expand the even moment under unit-volume cube integration. Odd-coordinate terms vanish, and each remaining term is nonnegative. The coordinate moments $1/12$, $1/80$ and $1/448$ are bounded by those of a centered Gaussian with variance $1/12$. Termwise comparison gives the stated constants. This is an integration identity for the operator, not a Gaussian model of the density.

446	\begin{proposition}[Integrated scalar remainder]
447	Under Proposition~2's density and pose classes, define
448	\begin{align}
449	L_p(k,q)&=2\pi(a\norm{k}c_p+s_t\norm{q}),\\
450	H_p(k)&=2\pi a^2\norm{k}c_p,\qquad T_2(k)=2\pi a^3\norm{k}c_2,\\
451	D(k,q)&=L_6(k,q)^3+3L_4(k,q)H_4(k)+T_2(k).
452	\end{align}
453	For $c_{iq}=(w_{R,iq}+iw_{I,iq})C_{iq}/\sigma$, the uniform scalar cubic remainder is bounded by
454	\begin{equation}\label{eq:momentremainder}
455	r_{\rm mom}(w)=\frac{B+P}{6}\sum_{i,q}|c_{iq}|D(k_{iq},q).
456	\end{equation}
457	It can replace the cubic term in Equation~\eqref{eq:continuouspose}, preserving the same conditional coverage guarantee.
458	\end{proposition}
459	\begin{proof}
460	Along a normalized pose segment, the phase $\phi(t,x)$ has derivative norms $\norm{\phi'}_p\le L_p$, $\norm{\phi''}_p\le H_p$ and $\norm{\phi'''}_2\le T_2$. This follows from $\norm{k^{(j)}(t)}\le a^j\norm{k}$ and linear detector translation. The exact third derivative of $e^{i\phi}$ is $e^{i\phi}(i\phi'''-3\phi'\phi''-i(\phi')^3)$. Minkowski and H\"older give its $L^2$ norm at most $D$. Triangle inequality with the fixed coefficients $c_{iq}$, Taylor's integral weight $1/6$, and Cauchy--Schwarz against a density of norm at most $B+P$ prove Equation~\eqref{eq:momentremainder}. Moreover, $\sum_q|c_{iq}|D_{iq}\le\norm{w_i}(\sum_q|C_{iq}/\sigma|^2D_{iq}^2)^{1/2}$, so retaining actual weights is no worse than this integrated Hilbert--Schmidt bound.
461	\end{proof}

466	\section{Uncertainty Targets in the Recent Literature}
467	The following distinctions guide baseline selection. They do not rank methods that solve different problems on one inappropriate score. The accompanying dated survey has 119 curated candidates across reconstruction, poses, heterogeneity, map validation, atomic ensembles and general inverse inference; its source manifest distinguishes retrieved material from targeted critical reading and inaccessible full text. This is a scoped critical survey rather than a claim to have exhaustively reviewed all cryo-EM applications. Versioned preprints are identified separately from published articles.
468	
469	\paragraph{Additional local and atomic validation.} The recent Gold-standard local toolbox compares half-map phase and amplitude, with explicit independent-noise assumptions in its SNR derivation \citep{goldlocal2026}. EMMIVox combines molecular force fields, map likelihoods and half-map-informed uncertainty for atomic refinement \citep{emmivox2024}. Neither output is the fixed raw-particle density functional studied here.
470	
471	\paragraph{Distributional inverse stability.} The recent revision of
472	\citet{stochastic2026} separates image-distribution discrepancy from latent
473	Wasserstein error under assumed local stability. Its observability inequality
474	bounds stability above, not below; it does not certify experimental coverage.
475	A correctly specified Gaussian-mixture baseline wins its matched synthetic
476	comparison, illustrating the importance of retaining favorable baselines.
477	
478	\paragraph{Direct statistical uncertainty prior art.} The probabilistic Fourier-slice model of \citet{ullrich2020} is a close reconstruction-uncertainty comparator and explicitly recognizes model bias. Joint likelihood soft modes \citep{rangan2024} expose pose--density ambiguities. \citet{lai2023} connect empirical Bayes and sequential MCMC filtering to dynamic image reconstruction, including scalar confidence sets and hybrid resampling. Their approximate fitted-family resampling and posterior computations differ from the present uniform conditional bounded-class statement; they cannot be dismissed as deterministic reconstruction methods. Neither general bias-aware inference nor the distinction between posterior variance and model error originates here.
479	
480	\paragraph{Latent orientations and moment validation.}
481	Nonuniform moment recovery has explicit bandlimit and genericity conditions;
482	numerical Jacobian ranks in unknown-law cases differ from exact uniqueness
483	proofs \citep{sharon2020}. SubspaceMoM compresses moments to jointly recover
484	structure and viewing laws, with its principal reconstruction tests on
485	synthetic CTF-corrupted images \citep{subspacemom2026}.
486	High-noise Fisher stratification for marginalized orbit likelihoods assumes
487	Haar rotations, generic signals and projected identifiability conditions
488	\citep{fan2024}; it is not per-particle pose calibration.
489	Moment-based structural comparison also profiles a viewing-law expansion
490	\citep{momentmetrics2024}. Its 10076 example uses separate states and deposited
491	shifts, with remaining acquisition effects and limited close-state discrimination.
492	These are substantive alternatives to conditional local-pose analysis, without
493	establishing the same finite-sample feature guarantee.
494	
495	Adjacent radiative CT work also separates analytic Gaussian uncertainty from shared reconstruction error and distinguishes foreground evaluation from whole-volume scores \citep{zhao2026radiative}. Its density-moment formulas and validation distinctions further constrain novelty claims; its acquisition and estimands differ from cryo-EM.
496	
497	Bayes' Rays uses post-hoc displacement uncertainty for a frozen NeRF, with a diagonal curvature approximation \citep{goli2024}. Its spatial target differs from an additive density interval. The dynamic extension proposed in \citet[Section 5.2]{patel2025thesis} is explicitly future work, with cryo-EM as an intended application; we do not treat that proposal as an experimentally validated density guarantee.
498	
499	\paragraph{Pose inference versus pose confidence.} Posterior-averaged orientation estimation \citep{bayespose2026} and probabilistic orientation search in SIMPLE \citep{simple2025} improve pose estimation through different statistical or optimization constructions. Neither an orientation distribution nor a stochastic search neighborhood should be relabeled a calibrated per-particle confidence ball without verifying its guarantee. Our prescribed local balls avoid that claim, but consequently do not solve practical pose calibration.
500	
501	Cryo-forum uses quaternion-distribution dispersion for error ranking and filtering \citep{cryoforum2023}. ARCHER learns reference-conditioned pose scores and evaluates cross-specimen transfer and junk rejection \citep{archer2026}. CESPED standardizes experimental poses obtained by refinement, and explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in those labels \citep{cesped2024}. CryoPARES transfers alignments between related experiments \citep{cryopares2026}; CryoFastAR combines multiview pose prediction, synthetic training and experimental fine-tuning \citep{cryofastar2025}. These approaches address efficiency and different transfer settings. Their quality scores and angular errors cannot supply a uniform maximum-error radius for every particle in a new stack. The $0.1^\circ$ and $0.5^\circ$ budgets in our frozen study are sensitivity settings, not experimentally established alignment accuracy.
502	
503	\paragraph{Physical heterogeneity versus estimation error.} RECOVAR estimates covariance and uses kernel regression to account for noisy latent coordinates \citep{recovar2025}. DynaMight and 3DFlex represent motion \citep{dynamight2024,flex2023}. Particle-counting work explicitly studies when assignments misestimate state populations \citep{counting2026}. These motivate separate tests of population recovery, structural variation and uncertainty in a homogeneous density. The present bounded-density target covers only the last. CryoDRGN-AI addresses joint ab initio reconstruction \citep{drgnai2025}; fixed-pose homogeneous training does not reproduce that task.
504	
505	DynaMight's held-out deformation disagreement and independent-half training assess motion errors; 3DFlex separates lower-frequency motion training from higher-frequency reconstruction validation. Their protocols must be examined at the level of shared components and evaluated frequencies. \citet{mattingly2026} study how the image model limits learnable conformational populations, using information-based selection of ensemble granularity. That prior-averaged population target differs from our fixed homogeneous density functional. CryoBench likewise distinguishes representation learning, conformation assignment and volume recovery with several reference-based FSC metrics \citep{cryobench2025}. Our simulations posit one density per acquisition geometry; the actual stacks need not be homogeneous. In particular, the assembly-intermediate mixture in EMPIAR-10076 does not validate our shared-density assumption.
506	
507	\paragraph{Map validation and learned priors.} False-discovery confidence maps test density significance against a noise reference \citep{beckers2019}. Directional resolution measures acquisition anisotropy \citep{monodir2020}; independent-particle tests assess map fit \citep{independent2020}. Bias/variance analyses explain why validation requires more than internal agreement \citep{sorzano2022}. Blush introduces learned reconstruction regularization \citep{blush2024}, while LocScale-2.0 attaches confidence to enhancement relative to its stated proxy \citep{locscale2026}. Compressed-image recovery with cryoSENSE targets acquisition fidelity rather than density-confidence coverage \citep{cryosense2026}. Matched evaluations must retain these targets. A sharper-looking map or a significant positive voxel is not itself a bound on error relative to unknown density.
508	
509	Fixed-candidate ensemble analysis also separates discretization bias, statistical variability and early stopping \citep{mordant2026}. Its simplified known-likelihood population problem differs from spatial density reconstruction with uncertain poses; it does not calibrate the nuisance bounds used here.
510	
511	CryoRes predicts local resolution using deposited and algorithm-derived training labels \citep{cryores2023}. Such supervision inherits the meaning of those labels; it does not transform a resolution score into a confidence interval. Similarly, held-out image prediction measures agreement with new observations, and can remain favorable when two reconstructions share unsupported density directions. Ground-truth simulation, new-exposure prediction, directional diagnostics and independent structural evidence therefore complement one another.
512	
513	\paragraph{Invariant compression and thermodynamic targets.} Moment-based posterior sampling conditions a learned prior on shift-invariant power spectra in one-dimensional orbit recovery \citep{janson2025}. Compression discards phase information, so posterior concentration can rely on the prior. Separately, cryoTWIN/PaStEL targets conformational free energies under sampling, pose and equilibrium assumptions \citep{cryotwin2026}. Neither problem is equivalent to our shared-density feature interval.
514	
515	\paragraph{Atomic ensembles and independent modalities.} Experiment-guided AlphaFold3 conditions structural generation on reconstructed ESP maps and other measurements \citep{guidedaf32026}. Its atomic-ensemble target differs from raw-particle density inference. The multimodal examples also illustrate why improved map agreement need not imply improved fit to a separate measurement modality. Independent evidence is relevant to assessing structural interpretations that the density measurements alone leave ambiguous.
516	
517	\paragraph{Coordinate-error conformal prediction.} CalPro calibrates protein-coordinate error scores at an exchangeable-protein level \citep{calpro2026}. Its atomic target and calibration unit differ from a fixed density feature inferred from noisy projections. We do not interpret a calibrated protein-average score as simultaneous residue coverage or as experimental-density coverage.
518	
519	\paragraph{Simultaneous inverse inference.} Constrained test-inversion methods already address joint confidence regions for multiple functionals \citep{batlle2025}. A single data-consistency region can support simultaneous projections, whereas separately calibrated marginal intervals generally require an appropriate correction. Our present scalar-target theorem is not a new general framework for simultaneous inference, and a colored map of marginal intervals must not be presented as simultaneous coverage.
520	
521	\paragraph{Conformal calibration and its sampling unit.} Posterior-variance calibration can provide error bounds even when a posterior sampler is approximate \citep{narnhofer2024}; its theorem uses independent identically distributed signal--observation pairs and conditions on a variance bin. QUTCC learns quantile-dependent image predictions and calibrates marginal pixel errors from paired reference images \citep{qutcc2026}. These methods can be useful without our fixed-signal radius assumption, but require a calibration population with the stated sampling relationship to deployment. Voxels or noise draws from one molecule are not automatically independent calibration molecules. Neither marginal population coverage nor variance-bin coverage is the same as coverage uniformly over every density in a specified class.
522	
523	\paragraph{Prior-assisted alignment and atomic refinement.} CryoPROS uses generated auxiliary particles for pose correction, with template-variation and noise-only controls \citep{cryopros2025}. Such tests address model bias without calibrating experimental pose confidence regions. CoCoFold fine-tunes AlphaFold against particle images using a Gaussian-mixture forward model and supplied poses/CTFs \citep{cocofold2026}. Its pose-perturbation checks support a sensitivity comparison, not a density-coverage guarantee. Both motivate independent validation of prior-assisted inference; neither is a matched density-functional uncertainty baseline here.
524	
525	\paragraph{Open questions suggested by the survey.} Particularly consequential gaps are absolute pose-confidence calibration under reference error; uncertainty in conformational populations when candidate structures are imperfect; validation of detail introduced by learned priors using independent particles; and uncertainty propagation through CTF fitting, image preprocessing, alignment and atomic interpretation. Acquisition chosen for a specific structural feature is another possible application of adjoint sensitivity. These are directions inferred from the literature, not priority claims or completed capabilities of this implementation. The present continuous audit addresses representation exclusion under stated nuisance assumptions; solving those assumptions empirically remains distinct work.

11	\subsection{Matrix-free shared fields and a numerical failure budget}
12	Each first or second pose-derivative field is a Fourier sum multiplied by one of
13	ten monomials $1,x,y,z,x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz$. Summing coefficient combinations
14	before transforming gives a field/adjoint pair with ten type-3 NUFFTs per
15	direction. No global particle-by-particle field Gram is formed. Positive group
16	scales $d_j$ may come from streamed block norms or from polynomial coefficient
17	envelopes. They need not equal exact block norms. Identically zero blocks may
18	be omitted; blocks that can become nonzero during optimization require positive
19	scales. Particle-specific pose radii are accepted.
20	
21	An approximate leading eigenvalue is insufficient for an upper audit. Random
22	starts have a long history in spectral estimation \citep{kw1992}; the following
23	elementary construction states our particular numerical probability budget.
24	For a fixed positive semidefinite $C=FF^\top$, draw $m$ independent standard
25	Gaussian probes $g_j$, independently of the estimator-selection process. Set
26	$c=\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(\delta^{1/m})$. Fix a leading unit
27	eigenvector $v$ before the draws. Since
28	\[
29	 \Pr\{\max_j|v^\top g_j|<c\}=\delta,
30	\]
31	with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every integer $p\ge1$,
32	\begin{equation}
33	 \lambda_{\max}(C)
34	 \le \left(\frac{\max_j\norm{C^p g_j}}{c}\right)^{1/p}.
35	 \label{eq:randompower}
36	\end{equation}
37	The proof retains the leading eigenvector component of $C^p g_j$ in its norm.
38	Stable normalization tracks the product of norms in log space. The minimum
39	across powers is valid on the same event; a deterministic trace bound may cap
40	it. A Rayleigh value is recorded only as a lower diagnostic.
41	
42	Add the analytic integration pad to this spectral upper value before using the
43	shared-field inequality. Allocate $\alpha_{\rm noise}+\delta\le\alpha$. A union
44	bound then includes numerical randomization in the stated failure budget.
45	Candidate selection using the same probes is not licensed: weights and scales
46	must be fixed before fresh final probes, or all candidates need a simultaneous
47	budget. Operator roundoff and NUFFT approximation remain numerical checks,
48	not validated arithmetic.

53	use different fitted estimators, so the latter result does not measure a

63	\subsection{Including pose uncertainty in estimator optimization}
64	Fix the group scales, let $F(w)$ be the scaled quadrature field matrix, and let
65	$a_q(w)$ be each real/imaginary weight pair's Euclidean amplitude. A nonnegative
66	matrix $M$ maps these amplitudes to polynomial coefficient envelopes. With
67	integration constant $E$, $R=B+P$, and integrated cubic coefficients $r_q\ge0$,
68	the revised sum objective is
69	\begin{align}
70	 J(w)&=z\norm{w}+B\norm{\ell-\A^*w}+p(w)
71	       +\sum_q r_q a_q(w),\nonumber\\
72	 p(w)&=R\sqrt{\sum_jd_j}
73	 \sqrt{\norm{F(w)}_{\rm op}^2+E\norm{Ma(w)}^2}.
74	 \label{eq:poseoptimized}
75	\end{align}
76	This is convex: $F$ is linear, $M$ is nonnegative, and the Euclidean norm is
77	monotone on the nonnegative orthant. It is an upper objective for the prescribed
78	class, not the exact minimax nonlinear-pose risk. Approximate singular modes
79	and log-sum-exp smoothing guide numerical optimization. The final primal upper
80	audit uses Equation~\eqref{eq:randompower} with fresh probes.
81	
82	A feasible dual lower bound remains available without an optimizer-success
83	claim. Choose $v\in H$ and supporting linear functionals $g_p,g_r$ such that
84	\begin{align*}
85	 \norm{v}&\le B,&\norm{\A v-g_p-g_r}&\le z,\\
86	 g_p^\top x&\le p(x),&
87	 g_r^\top x&\le\sum_qr_q a_q(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
88	\end{align*}
89	The four support inequalities in Equation~\eqref{eq:poseoptimized} yield
90	$J(x)\ge\ip{v}{\ell}$ by cancellation. Unit singular-direction outer products
91	and their convex mixtures have nuclear norm at most one, giving valid spectral
92	supports even when the selected modes are not leading. Coefficient and cubic
93	norm supports are combined with them. A padded continuous Gram-action error
94	bounds the remaining dual constraint; scaling all three dual quantities by
95	$\min(1,z/D)$ for an upper bound $D$ makes it feasible. The implementation

187	\paragraph{Retaining the density/pose cross term.}
188	Let $h=\ell-A_0^*w$ and write the existing nonlinear adjoint perturbation as
189	$D=Fv+e$, where $\norm v\le L=\sqrt{\sum d}$ and $\norm e\le r$.
190	Here each particle lies in the joint scaled five-dimensional unit ball.
191	Simultaneous maximal rotation and translation are excluded. For their product
192	set, replace $L^2$ by $2\sum_i d_i^{(1)}+4\sum_i d_i^{(2)}$ and scale $f$
193	by the corresponding radius ratio. The separate phase bounds in the cubic
194	remainder already cover either set. The two nuisance classes are reported
195	separately.
196	Suppose $f$ bounds $\norm{Fv}$ and $c$ bounds $\norm{F^*h}$.
197	The scalar bias for $\rho=\rho_0+u$ is
198	$\langle u,h-D\rangle-\langle\rho_0,D\rangle$. Thus
199	\begin{equation}
200	 b_{\rm joint}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}+Pf+(B+P)r
201	 \label{eq:joint-cross-bias}
202	\end{equation}
203	is an upper bound: expand $\norm{h-Fv}^2$, bound the cross term by $Lc$,
204	and apply Cauchy--Schwarz to $u$ and $\rho_0$. Take the minimum with the
205	preceding triangle bound on the same spectral event. This elementary
206	inequality is a post-audit refinement, not a new general theorem or a
207	claim that the expression is convex in $w$.
208	
209	Gaussian target moments evaluate $\langle\ell,F_j\rangle$ analytically
210	on the cube, including boundary terms. For
211	$I_j=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}x^jg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}\,dx$,
212	integration by parts gives
213	\begin{align*}
214	 I_1&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_0-s^2[g_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2},\\
215	 I_2&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_1+s^2I_0
216	       -s^2[xg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2}.
217	\end{align*}
218	For the finite Fourier-polynomial product $\langle A_0^*w,F_j\rangle$,
219	the existing quadrature error gives a cross-vector norm pad $ET\norm m$,
220	where $T$ is the absolute Fourier coefficient sum and $m$ contains the
221	scaled column coefficient bounds. Ordinary numerical roundoff remains
222	subject to the preceding caveat.
223	
224	Table~\ref{tab:joint-bias} retains the completed same-weight audits at
225	this revision cutoff; the machine-readable summary lists every attempt and
226	its source certificate seed. Each row uses its own source spectral event,
227	without selecting a minimum over repeated random certificates.
228	The 10076 half-degree conditional reference power increases from 0.670
229	to 0.968; the two-degree cut fit improves from width 0.689 to 0.598,
230	but its reference power remains negligible. The saved nonlinear feasible
231	stresses do not violate any new bound. This is evidence of reduced
232	conservatism on these cases, not experimental density coverage.
233	\input{tables/joint-bias}

235	An optional further constant refinement uses the sharp cube directional
236	moments $\sup_{\norm u=1}\mathbb{E}(u^\top X)^4=13/720$ and
237	$\sup_{\norm u=1}\mathbb{E}(u^\top X)^6=205/36288$, for uniform cube $X$.
238	Writing $p_j=u_j^2$, the sixth moment is
239	$5/576-\sum p_j^2/96+\sum p_j^3/252$; pairwise averaging maximizes it
240	at $p_j=1/3$. Replacing the earlier Gaussian moment majorants in the same
241	integrated remainder reduces the two-degree cut-fit width further to 0.572.
242	For the full-weight averaged fit, the joint and sharp-moment refinements give
243	widths 0.581 and 0.557, with feasible-over-upper ratios 0.582 and 0.608.
244	Expanding to the product pose set increases the latter width to 0.616; saved
245	joint-ball adversaries remain feasible examples but do not explore its extra
246	poses. Minimum reference sign power remains below $10^{-155}$ even for the
247	sharp joint-ball result. Independent tests exercise archive-scale Gaussian
248	moments, the analytic cross-product quadrature pad, and the distinction
249	between joint and product pose lifts. The original fit and every previous
250	bound are retained. Neither refinement establishes useful fine-feature
251	detection at one or two degrees.

253	\paragraph{Using the known pilot.}
254	The pilot term need not pay its full norm bound. If
255	$p\ge\norm{F^*\rho_0}$, Cauchy--Schwarz also gives
256	$|\langle\rho_0,Fv\rangle|\le Lp$. Hence the same spectral event supports
257	\begin{equation}
258	 b_{\rm pilot}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}
259	       +\min(Pf,Lp)+(B+P)r.
260	 \label{eq:pilot-cross-bias}
261	\end{equation}
262	The triangle alternative replaces the square root by $\norm h+f$;
263	their minimum remains valid. This changes neither the unknown density class
264	nor the weights. It is an elementary refinement of the known-function term,
265	not a new general coverage theorem or an optimization-gap certificate.
266	
267	For the known orthonormal constant-cell pilot on an $m^3$ grid, write
268	$x=c+z$ inside each cell. For a uniform offset
269	$z\in[-1/(2m),1/(2m)]$, with $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$,
270	\begin{align*}
271	 \mathbb E e^{2\pi i k z}&=\operatorname{sinc}(k/m),\\
272	 \mathbb E z e^{2\pi i k z}&=\frac{\operatorname{sinc}'(k/m)}{2\pi i m},\\
273	 \mathbb E z^2 e^{2\pi i k z}&=-\frac{\operatorname{sinc}''(k/m)}{4\pi^2m^2}.
274	\end{align*}
275	Expanding $x^\beta=(c+z)^\beta$ gives all ten degree-at-most-two
276	Fourier moments from ten transforms of center-weighted cell coefficients.
277	The orthonormal basis supplies $m^{-3/2}$ and the centered Fourier grid
278	requires phase $\exp(i\pi\sum_a k_a/m)$. Thus the known discontinuous
279	pilot is integrated over its cells, without replacing the unknown density
280	by a cell representation. Near zero we evaluate the sinc derivatives by
281	their Taylor series.
282	
283	Independent composite cell quadrature and nonlinear finite differences
284	check normalization and pose signs. Direct exponential sums over the actual
285	$24^3$ centers check all twenty lifted columns for three selected particles
286	in each of the first ten archived audits. The largest relative pairing
287	discrepancy is $3.49\times10^{-13}$; this selected-column check is not a
288	global floating-point error bound. The analytic formula has no quadrature
289	error, but its NUFFT and floating-point evaluation remain numerically
290	checked rather than interval-validated.
291	
292	Table~\ref{tab:pilot-pairing} reports this separate same-weight variant.
293	For the full-weight two-degree fit, the width falls from 0.557 to 0.510,
294	and the saved feasible-over-upper ratio rises to 0.667. Its minimum
295	reference sign power is still below $5\times10^{-122}$. The 10076 broad
296	central feature has power 0.997 at half a degree and 0.214 at one degree;
297	its two-degree width is 0.427, with negligible power. These conditional
298	improvements leave fine-scale usefulness and experimental calibration open.
299	\input{tables/pilot-pairing}
300	
301	\input{two-pose-methods}
302	
303	\subsection{An experimental noise-calibration attempt}
304	The following elementary conservative calculation allows nonzero calibration
305	signals. Suppose independent $Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\Sigma)$ have arbitrary fixed
306	means and a common covariance. Put $T=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ and
307	$S=\sum_i\norm{Y_i}^2$. For $\lambda>0$,
308	\begin{align*}
309	 \mathbb E e^{-\lambda S}
310	 &\le\det(I+2\lambda\Sigma)^{-n/2}\\
311	 &\le(1+2\lambda T)^{-n/2}.
312	\end{align*}
313	The first inequality follows from the noncentral Gaussian Laplace transform;
314	the second uses $\prod_j(1+x_j)\ge1+\sum_jx_j$ for nonnegative eigenvalues.
315	Optimizing the exponential Markov inequality gives
316	\[
317	 \Pr\{S\le ntT\}\le
318	 \exp\{n(1-t+\log t)/2\},\qquad 0<t<1.
319	\]
320	Choose $t$ to make the right side $\beta$. Then $T_+=S/(nt)$ is an upper bound
321	on $T$ with probability at least $1-\beta$, and $\Sigma\preceq T_+I$ on that
322	event. This can be much more conservative than estimating a known diagonal
323	noise model. Independent inference with the same covariance permits allocating
324	$\alpha_{\rm noise}+\beta\le\alpha$. The result does not prove the covariance
325	commonality or pose-independence assumptions for archive data.
326	
327	The exploratory three-stack attempt fits each old pilot's scalar amplitude on
328	pilot-pool particles, then calibrates from one particle per new exposure group.
329	Half of the new groups calibrate, and the others supply energy diagnostics.
330	Inference also uses one particle per old inference exposure group. No background
331	mask or fitted-signal subtraction enters the calibration statistic. We use
332	$\beta=0.005$, $\alpha_{\rm noise}=0.045$, density radius two, and prescribed
333	0/1/2-degree sensitivities with 0.5\,\AA\ shifts at nonzero angles.
334	
335	\input{tables/revision-experimental}
336	\begin{figure*}[t]
337	\centering\includegraphics[width=.98\textwidth]{figures/revision-experimental.pdf}
338	\caption{Experimental sensitivity intervals with one inference particle per
339	exposure group. Kernel widths are Gaussian standard deviations, not FSC
340	resolutions. None of these intervals excludes zero. All 10\,\AA\ targets switch
341	to the no-data center and width at nonzero pose budgets. Supplied density/pose
342	classes and unverified common-noise/consensus-pose assumptions preclude an
343	experimental coverage claim.}
344	\label{fig:revisionexperimental}
345	\end{figure*}
346	
347	All eighteen intervals contain their amplitude-aligned deposited-map value;
348	none excludes zero. This is a precision failure, not evidence of density
349	calibration. The 10\,\AA\ targets revert to no data at nonzero pose budgets.
350	The earlier 128-particle attempt on 10028 is also retained; it additionally
351	requires unverified independence within repeated exposure groups.
352	
353	\paragraph{Independent calibration in the estimator's directions.}
354	The trace envelope protects every direction, although a fixed feature estimator
355	needs only one scalar variance. Let $V$ contain its raw-coordinate particle
356	weight rows $v_i^\top$, chosen independently of a second calibration pool.
357	Under the same common-covariance and independence assumptions, its noise
358	variance is $s^2=\sum_i v_i^\top\Sigma v_i=\operatorname{tr}(V\Sigma V^\top)$.
359	Applying the preceding lemma to $VY_j$ gives the following direct corollary:
360	\[
361	 s^2\le s_+^2:=\frac{\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2}{nt}
362	 \quad\text{with probability at least }1-\beta.
363	\]
364	The projected coordinates may be correlated. Combining this event with the
365	bias-aware critical width at $\alpha_{\rm noise}$ gives pointwise failure at
366	most $\beta+\alpha_{\rm noise}$. Indeed, the width is at least the bias bound,
367	and its Gaussian outside probability increases with noise scale. This is an
368	elementary specialization of the trace argument, not a new concentration
369	principle or a simultaneous guarantee for selected targets.
370	
371	For the same calibration pool, $\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2\le
372	\norm{V}_F^2\sum_j\norm{Y_j}^2$, so directional calibration cannot exceed
373	the original trace envelope for these weights. To preserve independence here,
374	we retain weights selected using the original first exposure half and calibrate
375	their variance with the second half. The pools therefore differ in the empirical
376	comparison. Before projection, weights are pulled back through each particle's
377	known centering phase: complex coefficient $w_R+iw_I$ becomes
378	$\overline p(w_R+iw_I)/\sigma_{\rm old}$ in raw Fourier coordinates.
379	Ignoring this step would be incorrect for colored noise.
380	
381	\input{tables/directional-noise}
382	\begin{figure*}[t]
383	\centering\includegraphics[width=.98\textwidth]{figures/directional-noise.pdf}
384	\caption{All eighteen experimental directional-noise sensitivity cases.
385	Only the calibration bound changes; weights and continuous bias terms are
386	held fixed. The single interval excluding zero is the broad 10076 target at
387	fixed pose; it does not exclude zero at one degree. Noise, density and pose
388	assumptions remain unverified, and the previously inspected diagnostic pool
389	makes this exploratory reuse rather than a new frozen confirmation.}
390	\label{fig:directionalnoise}
391	\end{figure*}
392	
393	The new standard-deviation bounds are 0.132--0.285 times the original bounds.
394	One broad fixed-pose interval excludes zero; none does at one or two degrees.
395	Thus reducing this avoidable noise conservatism does not resolve the
396	pose/density precision problem. No experimental density-coverage inference
397	follows from deposited-map agreement or this conditional fixed-pose detection.
398	
399	\paragraph{Repeated particles within an inference exposure.}
400	The calibration can retain one independent representative per calibration
401	exposure while allowing arbitrary jointly Gaussian dependence among inference
402	particles from the same exposure. If exposure $g$ has $n_g$ particles and
403	$X_i=v_i^\top\epsilon_i$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
404	\[
405	 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in g}X_i\right)
406	 \le\left(\sum_{i\in g}\sqrt{v_i^\top\Sigma v_i}\right)^2
407	 \le n_g\sum_{i\in g}v_i^\top\Sigma v_i.
408	\]
409	Thus replace row $v_i$ of $V$ by $\sqrt{n_g}v_i$ in the trace calibration.
410	This elementary extension removes within-exposure independence; it retains
411	between-exposure independence, a common marginal raw covariance, Gaussianity,
412	and independence of the weights and supplied design from the relevant noise.
413	It does not establish those conditions for the archive particles.
414	
415	\paragraph{Refitting with an independent covariance guide.}
416	We also use the first exposure half's uncentered second moment $\widehat C$
417	to form $C=0.8\widehat C+0.2\operatorname{tr}(\widehat C)I/m$; the second half
418	still supplies the final directional noise bound. This positive matrix guides
419	optimization only. With known centering matrices $O_i$, set
420	$W=\operatorname{diag}_i[(O_iCO_i^\top)^{-1/2}]$ and write $w=Wx$.
421	The continuous fixed-pose problem then uses target vector $W\A\ell$ and Gram
422	$WGW$. Its proxy objective is $z\norm{x}+B\norm{\ell-\A^*Wx}$.
423	Quadrature residual errors are evaluated at $Wx$; transformed Gram-action
424	errors multiply by $\norm W$. None of these proxy quantities replaces the
425	independent final noise or pose audit.
426	
427	\input{tables/noise-metric-design}
428	All six proxy fits reach a sum-objective gap below 0.33\%. Their fixed-pose
429	intervals improve, but five one-degree intervals widen and the sixth remains
430	vacuous. Nine of eighteen settings now use no data, including every two-degree
431	setting. Only the same broad 10076 fixed-pose interval excludes zero. Thus
432	better noise-guided fixed-pose fitting can amplify pose sensitivity; it does
433	not substitute for joint pose-aware design.
434	
435	\paragraph{A larger physical 10\,\AA\ target.}
436	On 1,024 particles from 10049 at Fourier radius 12, with target Gaussian
437	standard deviation $10\,\AA$ and sampled band ending at $19.68\,\AA$, an order-80 continuous
438	fixed-pose fit reaches sum-objective gap 0.000992 in 3,583 seconds, with
439	relative half-width 0.01378. The independent normalized reference-map central
440	value is 1.9245; conditional sign power is one at fixed pose. Keeping those
441	weights and auditing a joint ball of one degree and $0.5\,\AA$ changes the
442	conclusion: even with sharp cube constants, residual cross terms and the
443	known-pilot refinement, the result uses the no-data interval and has zero
444	sign power. The polynomial pose term is 6.376 and the cubic remainder is
445	56.493; the final unselected half-width is 61.223, exceeding the no-data
446	half-width 34.390. The pose audit takes 1,491 seconds and 1.08 GB peak
447	resident memory. Thus increasing the particle count and band does not by
448	itself control the nonlinear remainder. These are conditional development
449	results under supplied noise and nuisance bounds; the 128- and 1,024-particle
450	subsets are not nested, and the latter fit is not pose-optimized.
451	
452	\input{enclosing-domain}
453	
454	\subsection{Uniform CTF sensitivities}
455	For fixed voltage, spherical aberration and amplitude contrast $a$,
456	$C=\sin(\gamma-\arcsin a)$. If each defocus axis can change by $d$ and its
457	astigmatism angle by $b$ radians, a conservative defocus error is
458	$d+|\mathrm{df}_U-\mathrm{df}_V|\sin(\min(b,\pi/2))$. Multiplying by
459	$\pi\lambda s^2$ and adding the phase-shift radius bounds the phase error.
460	Evaluate the exact sine range on that interval, then multiply by the positive
461	relative gain/B-factor range. This yields an absolute transfer envelope
462	$e_{iq}$ without division by a CTF zero.
463	
464	For any allowed pose, a complex Fourier wave has unit modulus on the unit-volume
465	cube. Therefore the additive CTF bias is bounded by
466	\begin{equation}
467	 b_{\rm CTF}\le (B+P)\sum_{iq}
468	       |w_{iq,\mathbb C}|e_{iq}/\sigma.
469	\end{equation}
470	This term can be combined with the nominal-CTF pose bound, including simultaneous
471	errors, but discards cancellations and is not optimized jointly with them.
472	Table~\ref{tab:revisionctf} applies it to all six saved radius-12 fixed-pose
473	fine-feature fits. Defocus uncertainty of 100\,\AA\ already causes two no-data
474	fallbacks; all six fall back at 500\,\AA\ and under the combined sensitivities.
475	These negative results diagnose a loose audit, not an impossibility theorem for
476	other estimators or a calibrated distribution of experimental CTF error.
477	\input{tables/revision-ctf}
478	
479	\subsection{An explicit support ablation}
480	Changing support changes the density class. For a centered cube of side
481	$s\le1$, the transformation $\widetilde\rho(u)=s^{3/2}\rho(su)$ is an $L^2$
482	isometry. The transformed acquisition uses $k'=sk$, $q'=sq$, $C'=s^{3/2}C$
483	and translation radius $t'=t/s$. A normalized Gaussian target uses center
484	$c/s$, width $\sigma_\ell/s$ and amplitude $s^{-3/2}$. Thus the target and
485	nonlinear acquisition values are preserved, including physical translations.
486	
487	Hard support need not be imposed without a sensitivity allowance. Write
488	$\rho=p_S+d_S+r_{S^c}$, where $p_S,d_S$ are supported inside the smaller cube,
489	$\norm{d_S}\le B$ and $\norm{r_{S^c}}\le\epsilon$. Add to the inside audit
490	\begin{align}
491	 b_{\rm tail}&\le\epsilon\left[\norm{\A_0^*w-\ell}
492	               +\sum_{iq}|c_{iq}|d_{iq}\right],\nonumber\\
493	 d_{iq}&=\min\!\left(2,2\pi\sqrt{
494	    \theta^2\norm{k_{iq}}^2/12+t^2\norm{q_{iq}}^2}\right).
495	\end{align}
496	Indeed, the spatial phase has zero mean on the cube, its integrated squared
497	linear part is $\norm{\Delta k}^2/12$, and the rotation chord is at most
498	$\theta\norm{k}$. Apply $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le\min(2,|a-b|)$ and the triangle
499	inequality, then restrict the residual to $S^c$. The bound is conservative;
500	it does not infer $\epsilon$ from the data.
501	
502	The initial radius-12, 10\,\AA\-sigma support probe on 10049 uses 128 particles,
503	$1^\circ$ and 0.5\,\AA\ translation. Side $s=0.5$ gives relative width 0.417
504	under hard support, yet the cropped-reference minimum sign power is below
505	$10^{-150}$. A tail radius of 0.1 causes no-data fallback. The original
506	unit-norm reference has outside norm 0.320 and is excluded by all these tail
507	settings; it is not relabeled as an in-class validation example. The completed
508	full-cube control takes 6,324 seconds, attains a fixed-pose sum-objective gap
509	of 0.19\%, and falls back to no data at every tested tail allowance after
510	adding pose sensitivity. Its integrated cubic term alone is 115.4 in the
511	normalized density units. A converged nominal fit therefore does not establish
512	a useful pose-aware interval.
513	
514	\paragraph{Signs and a total-norm bound.}
515	A separate same-weight ablation uses the alternative class
516	$\mathcal C(R,\eta)=\{f:\norm f\le R,\norm{f_-}\le\eta\}$,
517	where $0\le\eta\le R$ and $f_-=\max(-f,0)$. This is a different
518	origin-centered class, not a substituted radius in the old pilot interval.
519	For $h=\ell-\A_0^*w$, put $a=\norm{h_+}$ and $b=\norm{h_-}$.
520	Its elementary support function is
521	\[
522	 S_\eta(h)=\begin{cases}
523	 R\sqrt{a^2+b^2},& Rb\le\eta\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\\
524	 \sqrt{R^2-\eta^2}\,a+\eta b,&\text{otherwise}.
525	 \end{cases}
526	\]
527	The optimal positive/negative components align with $h_+$ and $h_-$;
528	maximizing their two norm contributions proves the formula. For an orthogonal
529	constant-cell projection $P_m$, Jensen gives
530	$\norm{(P_mh)_\pm}\le\norm{h_\pm}$. Combining these lower bounds with
531	the continuous $\norm h$ upper bound yields conservative support endpoints,
532	without restricting the unknown density to cells. If $U\ge S_\eta(h)$,
533	$L\ge S_\eta(-h)$ and the nuisance-field norm is at most $d$, the estimator
534	$w^\top y+(U-L)/2$ has bias at most $(U+L)/2+Rd$. The no-data interval
535	for our positive target is $[-\eta\norm\ell,R\norm\ell]$; both its center
536	and width replace the fitted interval on fallback. Projection error guards
537	are numerical checks, not validated floating-point bounds.
538	
539	We retain all $R=1,2,3$, $\eta/R=0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1$ and cell sizes
540	24, 48, 96 on the saved 1,024-particle, 10\,\AA\ 10049 fit. Its unit-normalized
541	processed reference has negative-part norm 0.4579, so several stronger sign
542	constraints exclude that comparator; this is not evidence about the sign of
543	the underlying physical density. At $R=1,\eta=0.5,m=96$, the nominal support
544	half-width decreases from 0.1090 to 0.1061. The inherited one-degree nuisance
545	field bound remains 9.1621 per unit density norm. All pose-sensitive cases
546	still have zero sign power, including every class containing the reference.
547	This diagnoses this same-weight bound, not impossibility under sign information
548	or an experimentally calibrated density norm.
549	
550	\input{cubic-pose-methods}
551	
552	\subsection{A closer Fourier variational comparison}
553	We independently implement the fixed-pose Gaussian variational objective of
554	\citet{ullrich2020}, Equation~14, in a Hermitian Fourier grid with trilinear
555	slice interpolation. The original authors' full software and pose-learning
556	pipeline are not reproduced. CTFs, an independent pilot as prior mean, physical
557	target normalization and a declared prior-scale sweep are explicit extensions.
558	For $x\sim N(m_0,\tau^2I)$ and whitened $y=Ax+e$, put
559	$Q=A^\top A+\tau^{-2}I$. The diagonal-Gaussian optimum has the full posterior
560	mean and coordinate variances $1/Q_{jj}$. A target's full posterior variance
561	is $\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell$, whereas its diagonal approximation is
562	$\sum_j\ell_j^2/Q_{jj}$. Differentiating the Gaussian objective verifies these
563	solutions without stochastic-training error. The identity
564	\[
565	 \norm{w}^2+\tau^2\norm{A^\top w-\ell}^2
566	   =\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell,\qquad w=AQ^{-1}\ell,
567	\]
568	separately checks prior-predictive calibration.
569	
570	Each stack uses 1,024 particles, radius 12 and two 10\,\AA\-sigma targets:
571	a central average and a contrast between centers at $z=\pm10$\,\AA.
572	The prior expected squared deviation norms are 0.25, 1 and 4; all settings
573	are retained. The sparse conditional calculations take 3.3--3.9 seconds per
574	stack and 45.0 MB per acquisition matrix. The full posterior's matched
575	prior-predictive coverage is 0.95, and the variance identity error is below
576	$4\times10^{-16}$. Diagonal feature intervals are \emph{wider} in every tested
577	case, by factors 1.073--1.415, with matched prior-predictive coverage
578	0.964--0.994. Diagonal covariance is therefore not a general explanation for
579	undercoverage of these targets.
580	
581	Table~\ref{tab:fouriervi} and Figure~\ref{fig:fouriervi} instead report
582	fixed-map, known-noise coverage. Interpolation and finite-representation forward
583	discrepancy is 16.8\%, 16.2\% and 25.3\% across the three reference generators.
584	Together with prior shrinkage, this is a material baseline limitation. These
585	controls do not refute Bayesian prior-predictive guarantees or constitute
586	experimental density-coverage measurements. All matched-model and nonlinear
587	pose controls are retained in the public records.
588	
589	We also audit each of these 18 estimators in the continuous cube without
590	changing its original affine center. Let $\kappa$ be the known difference
591	between its interpolated-prior center and the exact continuous-pilot center.
592	The fixed-pose bias bound is then $|\kappa|+2\norm{\ell-\A^*w}$. Audited
593	half-widths are 0.257--0.815 of no data and 56--352 times the original full
594	posterior widths. The nominal continuous-map checks are covered conservatively,
595	but sign power is numerically zero throughout, even after correcting
596	$\kappa$. Thus the broad continuous class already loses useful precision before
597	adding pose uncertainty. This does not establish impossibility for a physically
598	narrower class or a different estimator.
599	\input{tables/fourier-variational}
600	\begin{figure*}[t]
601	\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fourier-variational.pdf}
602	\caption{Known-noise coverage for fixed continuous reference densities at nominal
603	poses as the declared Gaussian prior scale varies. The dashed line is 0.95.
604	This is distinct from the full posterior's matched prior-predictive coverage,
605	which is 0.95 throughout. Diagonal VI is wider here; prior and forward-model
606	discrepancy remain important. No prior scale is selected using these outcomes.}
607	\label{fig:fouriervi}
608	\end{figure*}

\section{Development After Independent Review}\label{sec:revision}
The original frozen protocols and their outcomes are unchanged. This section
reports subsequent development, including negative experimental sensitivity
results. It does not establish that the current method meets the usefulness
requirements raised by the independent review.
The old frozen evaluators abort on detected undercoverage before retaining the
offending record. Neither completed study encountered that branch, but the
failure policy was flawed. Their source remains reproducible; new diagnostic
evaluators persist results before flagging an audit failure.

\subsection{Matrix-free shared fields and a numerical failure budget}
Each first or second pose-derivative field is a Fourier sum multiplied by one of
ten monomials $1,x,y,z,x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz$. Summing coefficient combinations
before transforming gives a field/adjoint pair with ten type-3 NUFFTs per
direction. No global particle-by-particle field Gram is formed. Positive group
scales $d_j$ may come from streamed block norms or from polynomial coefficient
envelopes. They need not equal exact block norms. Identically zero blocks may
be omitted; blocks that can become nonzero during optimization require positive
scales. Particle-specific pose radii are accepted.

An approximate leading eigenvalue is insufficient for an upper audit. Random
starts have a long history in spectral estimation \citep{kw1992}; the following
elementary construction states our particular numerical probability budget.
For a fixed positive semidefinite $C=FF^\top$, draw $m$ independent standard
Gaussian probes $g_j$, independently of the estimator-selection process. Set
$c=\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(\delta^{1/m})$. Fix a leading unit
eigenvector $v$ before the draws. Since
\[
 \Pr\{\max_j|v^\top g_j|<c\}=\delta,
\]
with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every integer $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_{\max}(C)
 \le \left(\frac{\max_j\norm{C^p g_j}}{c}\right)^{1/p}.
 \label{eq:randompower}
\end{equation}
The proof retains the leading eigenvector component of $C^p g_j$ in its norm.
Stable normalization tracks the product of norms in log space. The minimum
across powers is valid on the same event; a deterministic trace bound may cap
it. A Rayleigh value is recorded only as a lower diagnostic.

Add the analytic integration pad to this spectral upper value before using the
shared-field inequality. Allocate $\alpha_{\rm noise}+\delta\le\alpha$. A union
bound then includes numerical randomization in the stated failure budget.
Candidate selection using the same probes is not licensed: weights and scales
must be fixed before fresh final probes, or all candidates need a simultaneous
budget. Operator roundoff and NUFFT approximation remain numerical checks,
not validated arithmetic.

Completed radius-five audits with 128 and 1,024 particles take 50.3 and 353.3
seconds under concurrent Mac load, with measured peak resident memory of 390

\subsection{Including pose uncertainty in estimator optimization}
Fix the group scales, let $F(w)$ be the scaled quadrature field matrix, and let
$a_q(w)$ be each real/imaginary weight pair's Euclidean amplitude. A nonnegative
matrix $M$ maps these amplitudes to polynomial coefficient envelopes. With
integration constant $E$, $R=B+P$, and integrated cubic coefficients $r_q\ge0$,
the revised sum objective is
\begin{align}
 J(w)&=z\norm{w}+B\norm{\ell-\A^*w}+p(w)
       +\sum_q r_q a_q(w),\nonumber\\
 p(w)&=R\sqrt{\sum_jd_j}
 \sqrt{\norm{F(w)}_{\rm op}^2+E\norm{Ma(w)}^2}.
 \label{eq:poseoptimized}
\end{align}
This is convex: $F$ is linear, $M$ is nonnegative, and the Euclidean norm is
monotone on the nonnegative orthant. It is an upper objective for the prescribed
class, not the exact minimax nonlinear-pose risk. Approximate singular modes
and log-sum-exp smoothing guide numerical optimization. The final primal upper
audit uses Equation~\eqref{eq:randompower} with fresh probes.

A feasible dual lower bound remains available without an optimizer-success
claim. Choose $v\in H$ and supporting linear functionals $g_p,g_r$ such that
\begin{align*}
 \norm{v}&\le B,&\norm{\A v-g_p-g_r}&\le z,\\
 g_p^\top x&\le p(x),&
 g_r^\top x&\le\sum_qr_q a_q(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
\end{align*}
The four support inequalities in Equation~\eqref{eq:poseoptimized} yield
$J(x)\ge\ip{v}{\ell}$ by cancellation. Unit singular-direction outer products
and their convex mixtures have nuclear norm at most one, giving valid spectral
supports even when the selected modes are not leading. Coefficient and cubic
norm supports are combined with them. A padded continuous Gram-action error
bounds the remaining dual constraint; scaling all three dual quantities by
$\min(1,z/D)$ for an upper bound $D$ makes it feasible. The implementation
details and full support argument are recorded with the source.

\paragraph{Retaining the density/pose cross term.}
Let $h=\ell-A_0^*w$ and write the existing nonlinear adjoint perturbation as
$D=Fv+e$, where $\norm v\le L=\sqrt{\sum d}$ and $\norm e\le r$.
Here each particle lies in the joint scaled five-dimensional unit ball.
Simultaneous maximal rotation and translation are excluded. For their product
set, replace $L^2$ by $2\sum_i d_i^{(1)}+4\sum_i d_i^{(2)}$ and scale $f$
by the corresponding radius ratio. The separate phase bounds in the cubic
remainder already cover either set. The two nuisance classes are reported
separately.
Suppose $f$ bounds $\norm{Fv}$ and $c$ bounds $\norm{F^*h}$.
The scalar bias for $\rho=\rho_0+u$ is
$\langle u,h-D\rangle-\langle\rho_0,D\rangle$. Thus
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm joint}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}+Pf+(B+P)r
 \label{eq:joint-cross-bias}
\end{equation}
is an upper bound: expand $\norm{h-Fv}^2$, bound the cross term by $Lc$,
and apply Cauchy--Schwarz to $u$ and $\rho_0$. Take the minimum with the
preceding triangle bound on the same spectral event. This elementary
inequality is a post-audit refinement, not a new general theorem or a
claim that the expression is convex in $w$.

Gaussian target moments evaluate $\langle\ell,F_j\rangle$ analytically
on the cube, including boundary terms. For
$I_j=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}x^jg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}\,dx$,
integration by parts gives
\begin{align*}
 I_1&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_0-s^2[g_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2},\\
 I_2&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_1+s^2I_0
       -s^2[xg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
For the finite Fourier-polynomial product $\langle A_0^*w,F_j\rangle$,
the existing quadrature error gives a cross-vector norm pad $ET\norm m$,
where $T$ is the absolute Fourier coefficient sum and $m$ contains the
scaled column coefficient bounds. Ordinary numerical roundoff remains
subject to the preceding caveat.

\paragraph{Using the known pilot.}
The pilot term need not pay its full norm bound. If
$p\ge\norm{F^*\rho_0}$, Cauchy--Schwarz also gives
$|\langle\rho_0,Fv\rangle|\le Lp$. Hence the same spectral event supports
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm pilot}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}
       +\min(Pf,Lp)+(B+P)r.
 \label{eq:pilot-cross-bias}
\end{equation}
The triangle alternative replaces the square root by $\norm h+f$;
their minimum remains valid. This changes neither the unknown density class
nor the weights. It is an elementary refinement of the known-function term,
not a new general coverage theorem or an optimization-gap certificate.

For the known orthonormal constant-cell pilot on an $m^3$ grid, write
$x=c+z$ inside each cell. For a uniform offset
$z\in[-1/(2m),1/(2m)]$, with $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E e^{2\pi i k z}&=\operatorname{sinc}(k/m),\\
 \mathbb E z e^{2\pi i k z}&=\frac{\operatorname{sinc}'(k/m)}{2\pi i m},\\
 \mathbb E z^2 e^{2\pi i k z}&=-\frac{\operatorname{sinc}''(k/m)}{4\pi^2m^2}.
\end{align*}
Expanding $x^\beta=(c+z)^\beta$ gives all ten degree-at-most-two
Fourier moments from ten transforms of center-weighted cell coefficients.
The orthonormal basis supplies $m^{-3/2}$ and the centered Fourier grid
requires phase $\exp(i\pi\sum_a k_a/m)$. Thus the known discontinuous
pilot is integrated over its cells, without replacing the unknown density
by a cell representation. Near zero we evaluate the sinc derivatives by
their Taylor series.

\subsection{An experimental noise-calibration attempt}
The following elementary conservative calculation allows nonzero calibration
signals. Suppose independent $Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\Sigma)$ have arbitrary fixed
means and a common covariance. Put $T=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ and
$S=\sum_i\norm{Y_i}^2$. For $\lambda>0$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E e^{-\lambda S}
 &\le\det(I+2\lambda\Sigma)^{-n/2}\\
 &\le(1+2\lambda T)^{-n/2}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the noncentral Gaussian Laplace transform;
the second uses $\prod_j(1+x_j)\ge1+\sum_jx_j$ for nonnegative eigenvalues.
Optimizing the exponential Markov inequality gives
\[
 \Pr\{S\le ntT\}\le
 \exp\{n(1-t+\log t)/2\},\qquad 0<t<1.
\]
Choose $t$ to make the right side $\beta$. Then $T_+=S/(nt)$ is an upper bound
on $T$ with probability at least $1-\beta$, and $\Sigma\preceq T_+I$ on that
event. This can be much more conservative than estimating a known diagonal
noise model. Independent inference with the same covariance permits allocating
$\alpha_{\rm noise}+\beta\le\alpha$. The result does not prove the covariance
commonality or pose-independence assumptions for archive data.

The exploratory three-stack attempt fits each old pilot's scalar amplitude on
pilot-pool particles, then calibrates from one particle per new exposure group.
Half of the new groups calibrate, and the others supply energy diagnostics.
Inference also uses one particle per old inference exposure group. No background
mask or fitted-signal subtraction enters the calibration statistic. We use
$\beta=0.005$, $\alpha_{\rm noise}=0.045$, density radius two, and prescribed
0/1/2-degree sensitivities with 0.5\,\AA\ shifts at nonzero angles.

\paragraph{Independent calibration in the estimator's directions.}
The trace envelope protects every direction, although a fixed feature estimator
needs only one scalar variance. Let $V$ contain its raw-coordinate particle
weight rows $v_i^\top$, chosen independently of a second calibration pool.
Under the same common-covariance and independence assumptions, its noise
variance is $s^2=\sum_i v_i^\top\Sigma v_i=\operatorname{tr}(V\Sigma V^\top)$.
Applying the preceding lemma to $VY_j$ gives the following direct corollary:
\[
 s^2\le s_+^2:=\frac{\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2}{nt}
 \quad\text{with probability at least }1-\beta.
\]
The projected coordinates may be correlated. Combining this event with the
bias-aware critical width at $\alpha_{\rm noise}$ gives pointwise failure at
most $\beta+\alpha_{\rm noise}$. Indeed, the width is at least the bias bound,
and its Gaussian outside probability increases with noise scale. This is an
elementary specialization of the trace argument, not a new concentration
principle or a simultaneous guarantee for selected targets.

For the same calibration pool, $\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2\le
\norm{V}_F^2\sum_j\norm{Y_j}^2$, so directional calibration cannot exceed
the original trace envelope for these weights. To preserve independence here,
we retain weights selected using the original first exposure half and calibrate
their variance with the second half. The pools therefore differ in the empirical
comparison. Before projection, weights are pulled back through each particle's
known centering phase: complex coefficient $w_R+iw_I$ becomes
$\overline p(w_R+iw_I)/\sigma_{\rm old}$ in raw Fourier coordinates.
Ignoring this step would be incorrect for colored noise.

particles from the same exposure. If exposure $g$ has $n_g$ particles and

independent final noise or pose audit.

\subsection{Uniform CTF sensitivities}
For fixed voltage, spherical aberration and amplitude contrast $a$,
$C=\sin(\gamma-\arcsin a)$. If each defocus axis can change by $d$ and its
astigmatism angle by $b$ radians, a conservative defocus error is
$d+|\mathrm{df}_U-\mathrm{df}_V|\sin(\min(b,\pi/2))$. Multiplying by
$\pi\lambda s^2$ and adding the phase-shift radius bounds the phase error.
Evaluate the exact sine range on that interval, then multiply by the positive
relative gain/B-factor range. This yields an absolute transfer envelope
$e_{iq}$ without division by a CTF zero.

For any allowed pose, a complex Fourier wave has unit modulus on the unit-volume
cube. Therefore the additive CTF bias is bounded by
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm CTF}\le (B+P)\sum_{iq}
       |w_{iq,\mathbb C}|e_{iq}/\sigma.
\end{equation}
This term can be combined with the nominal-CTF pose bound, including simultaneous
errors, but discards cancellations and is not optimized jointly with them.
Table~\ref{tab:revisionctf} applies it to all six saved radius-12 fixed-pose
fine-feature fits. Defocus uncertainty of 100\,\AA\ already causes two no-data
fallbacks; all six fall back at 500\,\AA\ and under the combined sensitivities.
These negative results diagnose a loose audit, not an impossibility theorem for
other estimators or a calibrated distribution of experimental CTF error.

\subsection{An explicit support ablation}
Changing support changes the density class. For a centered cube of side
$s\le1$, the transformation $\widetilde\rho(u)=s^{3/2}\rho(su)$ is an $L^2$
isometry. The transformed acquisition uses $k'=sk$, $q'=sq$, $C'=s^{3/2}C$
and translation radius $t'=t/s$. A normalized Gaussian target uses center
$c/s$, width $\sigma_\ell/s$ and amplitude $s^{-3/2}$. Thus the target and
nonlinear acquisition values are preserved, including physical translations.

Hard support need not be imposed without a sensitivity allowance. Write
$\rho=p_S+d_S+r_{S^c}$, where $p_S,d_S$ are supported inside the smaller cube,
$\norm{d_S}\le B$ and $\norm{r_{S^c}}\le\epsilon$. Add to the inside audit
\begin{align}
 b_{\rm tail}&\le\epsilon\left[\norm{\A_0^*w-\ell}
               +\sum_{iq}|c_{iq}|d_{iq}\right],\nonumber\\
 d_{iq}&=\min\!\left(2,2\pi\sqrt{
    \theta^2\norm{k_{iq}}^2/12+t^2\norm{q_{iq}}^2}\right).
\end{align}
Indeed, the spatial phase has zero mean on the cube, its integrated squared
linear part is $\norm{\Delta k}^2/12$, and the rotation chord is at most
$\theta\norm{k}$. Apply $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le\min(2,|a-b|)$ and the triangle
inequality, then restrict the residual to $S^c$. The bound is conservative;
it does not infer $\epsilon$ from the data.

The initial radius-12, 10\,\AA\-sigma support probe on 10049 uses 128 particles,
$1^\circ$ and 0.5\,\AA\ translation. Side $s=0.5$ gives relative width 0.417
under hard support, yet the cropped-reference minimum sign power is below
$10^{-150}$. A tail radius of 0.1 causes no-data fallback. The original
unit-norm reference has outside norm 0.320 and is excluded by all these tail
settings; it is not relabeled as an in-class validation example. The completed
full-cube control takes 6,324 seconds, attains a fixed-pose sum-objective gap
of 0.19\%, and falls back to no data at every tested tail allowance after
adding pose sensitivity. Its integrated cubic term alone is 115.4 in the
normalized density units. A converged nominal fit therefore does not establish
a useful pose-aware interval.

\paragraph{Signs and a total-norm bound.}
A separate same-weight ablation uses the alternative class
$\mathcal C(R,\eta)=\{f:\norm f\le R,\norm{f_-}\le\eta\}$,
where $0\le\eta\le R$ and $f_-=\max(-f,0)$. This is a different
origin-centered class, not a substituted radius in the old pilot interval.
For $h=\ell-\A_0^*w$, put $a=\norm{h_+}$ and $b=\norm{h_-}$.
Its elementary support function is
\[
 S_\eta(h)=\begin{cases}
 R\sqrt{a^2+b^2},& Rb\le\eta\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\\
 \sqrt{R^2-\eta^2}\,a+\eta b,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The optimal positive/negative components align with $h_+$ and $h_-$;
maximizing their two norm contributions proves the formula. For an orthogonal
constant-cell projection $P_m$, Jensen gives
$\norm{(P_mh)_\pm}\le\norm{h_\pm}$. Combining these lower bounds with
the continuous $\norm h$ upper bound yields conservative support endpoints,
without restricting the unknown density to cells. If $U\ge S_\eta(h)$,
$L\ge S_\eta(-h)$ and the nuisance-field norm is at most $d$, the estimator
$w^\top y+(U-L)/2$ has bias at most $(U+L)/2+Rd$. The no-data interval
for our positive target is $[-\eta\norm\ell,R\norm\ell]$; both its center
and width replace the fitted interval on fallback. Projection error guards
are numerical checks, not validated floating-point bounds.

We retain all $R=1,2,3$, $\eta/R=0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1$ and cell sizes
24, 48, 96 on the saved 1,024-particle, 10\,\AA\ 10049 fit. Its unit-normalized
processed reference has negative-part norm 0.4579, so several stronger sign
constraints exclude that comparator; this is not evidence about the sign of
the underlying physical density. At $R=1,\eta=0.5,m=96$, the nominal support
half-width decreases from 0.1090 to 0.1061. The inherited one-degree nuisance
field bound remains 9.1621 per unit density norm. All pose-sensitive cases
still have zero sign power, including every class containing the reference.

\subsection{A closer Fourier variational comparison}
We independently implement the fixed-pose Gaussian variational objective of
\citet{ullrich2020}, Equation~14, in a Hermitian Fourier grid with trilinear
slice interpolation. The original authors' full software and pose-learning
pipeline are not reproduced. CTFs, an independent pilot as prior mean, physical
target normalization and a declared prior-scale sweep are explicit extensions.
For $x\sim N(m_0,\tau^2I)$ and whitened $y=Ax+e$, put
$Q=A^\top A+\tau^{-2}I$. The diagonal-Gaussian optimum has the full posterior
mean and coordinate variances $1/Q_{jj}$. A target's full posterior variance
is $\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell$, whereas its diagonal approximation is
$\sum_j\ell_j^2/Q_{jj}$. Differentiating the Gaussian objective verifies these
solutions without stochastic-training error. The identity
\[
 \norm{w}^2+\tau^2\norm{A^\top w-\ell}^2
   =\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell,\qquad w=AQ^{-1}\ell,
\]
separately checks prior-predictive calibration.

Each stack uses 1,024 particles, radius 12 and two 10\,\AA\-sigma targets:
a central average and a contrast between centers at $z=\pm10$\,\AA.
The prior expected squared deviation norms are 0.25, 1 and 4; all settings
are retained. The sparse conditional calculations take 3.3--3.9 seconds per
stack and 45.0 MB per acquisition matrix. The full posterior's matched
prior-predictive coverage is 0.95, and the variance identity error is below
$4\times10^{-16}$. Diagonal feature intervals are \emph{wider} in every tested
case, by factors 1.073--1.415, with matched prior-predictive coverage
0.964--0.994. Diagonal covariance is therefore not a general explanation for
undercoverage of these targets.

Table~\ref{tab:fouriervi} and Figure~\ref{fig:fouriervi} instead report
fixed-map, known-noise coverage. Interpolation and finite-representation forward
discrepancy is 16.8\%, 16.2\% and 25.3\% across the three reference generators.
Together with prior shrinkage, this is a material baseline limitation. These
controls do not refute Bayesian prior-predictive guarantees or constitute
experimental density-coverage measurements. All matched-model and nonlinear
pose controls are retained in the public records.

We also audit each of these 18 estimators in the continuous cube without
changing its original affine center. Let $\kappa$ be the known difference
between its interpolated-prior center and the exact continuous-pilot center.
The fixed-pose bias bound is then $|\kappa|+2\norm{\ell-\A^*w}$. Audited
half-widths are 0.257--0.815 of no data and 56--352 times the original full
posterior widths. The nominal continuous-map checks are covered conservatively,
but sign power is numerically zero throughout, even after correcting
$\kappa$. Thus the broad continuous class already loses useful precision before
adding pose uncertainty. This does not establish impossibility for a physically
narrower class or a different estimator.

1	\subsection{Constructive ambiguity from two feasible pose designs}
2	Wide upper bounds alone cannot distinguish intrinsic ambiguity from a loose
3	audit. We therefore construct lower bounds from two allowed pose designs,
4	using the classical Gaussian testing argument \citep{donoho1994}. This is a
5	diagnostic on the same declared class, not a new minimax principle.
6	
7	Let $A_0,A_1$ be two allowed observation operators, and let
8	$\rho_j$ belong to $\mathcal C=\{\rho:\norm{\rho-\rho_0^{\rm pilot}}\le B\}$.
9	Both designs have identity observation covariance. If
10	\begin{equation}
11	 D=\norm{A_1\rho_1-A_0\rho_0}<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha),
12	 \label{eq:two-pose-distance}
13	\end{equation}
14	then every uniformly $1-\alpha$ valid interval whose length is deterministic
15	must have half-length at least
16	$|\langle\ell,\rho_1-\rho_0\rangle|/2$. Indeed, if a shorter interval
17	contained either feature with probability at least $1-\alpha$, its membership
18	test for one feature would distinguish the two hypotheses with both error
19	probabilities at most $\alpha$. The minimum sum of errors for their Gaussian
20	distributions is $2\Phi(-D/2)>2\alpha$, a contradiction. This conclusion does
21	not bound the expected length of arbitrary variable-length intervals.
22	
23	Write $p=A_1\rho_0^{\rm pilot}-A_0\rho_0^{\rm pilot}$ and choose a distance
24	budget $\tau<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$. For any observation weights $w$,
25	\begin{equation}

\subsection{Constructive ambiguity from two feasible pose designs}
Wide upper bounds alone cannot distinguish intrinsic ambiguity from a loose
audit. We therefore construct lower bounds from two allowed pose designs,
using the classical Gaussian testing argument \citep{donoho1994}. This is a
diagnostic on the same declared class, not a new minimax principle.

Let $A_0,A_1$ be two allowed observation operators, and let
$\rho_j$ belong to $\mathcal C=\{\rho:\norm{\rho-\rho_0^{\rm pilot}}\le B\}$.
Both designs have identity observation covariance. If
\begin{equation}
 D=\norm{A_1\rho_1-A_0\rho_0}<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha),
 \label{eq:two-pose-distance}
\end{equation}
then every uniformly $1-\alpha$ valid interval whose length is deterministic
must have half-length at least
$|\langle\ell,\rho_1-\rho_0\rangle|/2$. Indeed, if a shorter interval
contained either feature with probability at least $1-\alpha$, its membership
test for one feature would distinguish the two hypotheses with both error
probabilities at most $\alpha$. The minimum sum of errors for their Gaussian
distributions is $2\Phi(-D/2)>2\alpha$, a contradiction. This conclusion does
not bound the expected length of arbitrary variable-length intervals.

Write $p=A_1\rho_0^{\rm pilot}-A_0\rho_0^{\rm pilot}$ and choose a distance
budget $\tau<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$. For any observation weights $w$,
\begin{equation}
 G(w)=B\sum_{j=0}^1\norm{\ell-A_j^*w}-w^\top p+\tau\norm w
 \label{eq:two-pose-dual}
\end{equation}
upper-bounds the largest feasible feature gap for this fixed pair of pose
designs. To see this, insert $A_j^*w$ into the two feature pairings, apply
the density-ball bounds, and use
$w^\top(A_1\rho_1-A_0\rho_0)\le\tau\norm w$.

The same weights yield explicit continuous witnesses. Put
$h_j=\ell-A_j^*w$, choose $r_j\ge\norm{h_j}$, and set
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde\rho_1=\rho_0^{\rm pilot}+Bh_1/r_1,\qquad
 \widetilde\rho_0=\rho_0^{\rm pilot}-Bh_0/r_0.
\end{equation}
If $r_j=0$, its perturbation is set to zero. Their mean difference is
$p+\sum_j(B/r_j)(A_j\ell-A_jA_j^*w)$ and their feature difference is
$\sum_j(B/r_j)(\norm\ell^2-w^\top A_j\ell)$. Let $\overline D$ bound the
mean-distance norm. Multiplying both densities by
$\lambda=\min(1,\tau/\overline D)$ (one if $\overline D=0$) makes them feasible for
Equation~\eqref{eq:two-pose-distance}. This scaling preserves the original
class when $\norm{\rho_0^{\rm pilot}}\le B$, because zero is in the ball
and the ball is convex. Thus the scaled feature gap supplies a constructive
lower bound even if optimization is incomplete.

We minimize Equation~\eqref{eq:two-pose-dual} by iteratively reweighted
quadratic solves and retain both the best feasible pair and the best dual
weights, which may occur at different iterations. Continuous Gram integration
errors pad each residual norm and the mean-distance norm. Translation is a
real orthogonal rotation of each Fourier cosine/sine pair, so the phase-wrapped
Gram and target preserve those error norms. The witnesses are continuous
target/adjoint fields plus the known pilot; they are not restricted to a voxel
representation. Floating-point magnitude guards are additional numerical
checks, not validated interval arithmetic.

The prespecified development grid uses the existing 128-particle, radius-5
geometries and broad targets on three stacks. It includes identical nominal
poses, antipodal coherent rotations, and antipodal random joint-ball poses at
one and two degrees with $0.5\,\AA$ translation radius. The same random unit
vectors are used at both angular budgets. Independent conic programs check
small Hilbert-space cases; deliberately crude quadrature is checked against
the exact continuous sinc Gram; nonlinear constant-cell projections check
the phase convention. A serialization failure and the first complete grid
remain archived. The final rerun adds the numerical guards and separate
witness records requested by the focused mathematical audit.

ambiguity, so these results do not prove that the larger upper bounds can be
attained or substantially reduced. The testing statement also retains the
declared white-Gaussian noise, density and nuisance assumptions.

\paragraph{A bounded alternating ambiguity probe.}
We next test whether changing the selected poses strengthens a witness, using
one prespecified 10049 central-feature case at two degrees and $0.5\,\AA$.
Project the two unscaled continuous densities onto a nested constant-cell basis
containing the original pilot. Orthogonal projection cannot increase their

Refitting the continuous densities at the 72-cell step's poses raises the

protocol raise it to 0.14594 and 0.14962, with final fixed-pair bracket gap
0.1422\%. We stop at the specified three rounds. This is a stronger selected
witness, not a global ambiguity limit. The
projected densities carry substantial negative-value energy (approximately

containing the approximate reference. This is sensitivity to a comparison
frame, not improved estimation or density calibration.

On the already selected 10049 region 1, minimum simulated sign power across
the three declared poses changes from 0.00654 to 0.95725 for the original
cubic estimator, from $7.73\times10^{-7}$ to 0.26042 for the coordinate design,
and from 0.00663 to 0.95770 for the reduced-subspace design. Their widths do
not change. Original and reduced-subspace weights are identical to numerical
precision; separate numerical audits explain their small width difference.
The larger power results from the generator's frame and does not resolve the
optimization gap, the 20\,\AA\ target scale, or experimental input conditions.

\paragraph{Experimental cubic application.}
Another declared protocol then applies all three completed cubic estimators
to the original inference images using the previously collected 128
noise-calibration exposure representatives. It replays the published fixed
estimator's observed center, calibrated standard deviation and half-width
before computing new outcomes. The group-noise bound permits arbitrary
within-exposure dependence: these 128 inference particles occupy only 26
exposures, with maximum group size twelve. The Gaussian tail, calibration
and spectral allowances are $(.045-10^{-6})/12$, $.005/12$ and $10^{-6}/12$ per
procedure. Under the required fixed-design assumptions, a union bound for
these three alternatives is $.0125$; inspected-data reuse precludes treating
this calculation as fresh experimental coverage validation.

The original cubic center is 2.46178 and its half-width is 4.30107 (0.35374
of no data). The coordinate design gives $2.48844\pm4.82603$ (0.39692), and
the reduced-subspace design gives $2.46178\pm4.29998$ (0.35365). None excludes
zero or uses the no-data fallback. All contain the registered approximate
target 2.48846 and the old-frame target 0.71012. The original cubic noise SD
upper is 1.01002, 4.55146 times its supplied simulation SD. These results
locate a practical obstacle: useful power under supplied noise does not
transfer to this experimental noise bound. Reference inclusion is only
agreement, and the underlying pose, covariance and density-class conditions
remain unverified. Both protocols, all alternatives and exact arrays are kept.

\paragraph{Centered calibration with arbitrary means.}
The uncentered SD bound includes signal energy. A separately declared follow-up
uses fixed orthogonal contrasts to remove a common component. If independent
rows satisfy $Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\Sigma)$ with arbitrary fixed means, choose
$Q\in\mathbb R^{(n-1)\times n}$ with $QQ^\top=I$ and $Q\mathbf1=0$.
Rows of $QY$ are independent Gaussian vectors with covariance $\Sigma$:
their cross-covariance is $(QQ^\top)_{ij}\Sigma$. Their means need not vanish.
The previous noncentral trace bound therefore applies with $n-1$ rows, and
$\|QY\|_F^2=\sum_i\|Y_i-\bar Y\|^2$. Apply the same contrast to the
group-inflated weight projections. This is a classical Gaussian orthogonal-
contrast argument, not a new general coverage principle. The matrix $Q$ is
fixed; an image-fitted contrast would need separate justification.

All uncentered SD bounds replay before this follow-up. On the same inspected
calibration cohorts, centered/uncentered SD ratios are 0.437--0.823 across all
twelve fixed estimators. Fixed-pose zero exclusions increase from six to ten
and shift-only exclusions from four to six; rotational exclusions remain zero
and all sixteen no-data fallbacks remain. Five registered reference targets
now lie outside: 10076 regions 1 and 3 at fixed/shift-only poses, and its
matched center at fixed poses. The other 43 fixed-weight intervals contain
the reference. This is disagreement with one Class A assembly state, not
a ground-truth coverage label for the heterogeneous population. Original, coordinate and reduced-subspace cubic intervals
become $2.46178\pm3.07893$, $2.48844\pm3.60408$ and $2.46178\pm3.07784$,
respectively. None excludes zero. For the original cubic fit, the SD upper
falls from 1.01002 to 0.55294, still exceeding the supplied simulation SD
0.22191. A smaller bound does not identify pure noise or establish the
experimental assumptions. The two procedures are separately reported
alternatives; their unadjusted minimum is never used.

The later enriched and joint designs are applied under a separate declared
four-interval protocol with the same per-procedure allocations and replay
checks. The enriched estimator gives $2.46350\pm4.28261$ under raw calibration
and $2.46350\pm3.06013$ after centering. The joint estimator gives
$2.46896\pm4.21952$ and $2.46896\pm3.01088$, respectively. All four contain
zero and both reference values, without fallback. Centered SD upper bounds
are 0.55211/0.54519, compared with supplied simulation SDs 0.22166/0.21869.
Thus the 0.79\%/2.55\% simulation-width improvements do not remedy the
experimental limitation (Figure~\ref{fig:cubiccomparison}). These remain
reused-data alternatives, without a simultaneous claim across the history
of development procedures.


\paragraph{A finite family of projected calibration designs.}
A further declared diagnostic compares seven noise-independent orthogonal
contrasts: no projection, mean removal, two CTF-design spans and three
pilot-prediction spans. Each bound receives $\beta/7$, so their minimum
retains the original total allowance by a union bound under the same Gaussian
and fixed-design premises. Every contrast is retained. Selected SD bounds
are 0.981--1.030 times the separately reported centered bounds: four fixed
estimators improve and eight worsen. Exclusion counts and the five Class A
reference disagreements are unchanged. Cubic half-widths are 3.11643,
3.64233 and 3.11534, all slightly worse than centering alone. This diagnostic
does not improve experimental conclusions. Upstream metadata independence
remains unverified, and no unadjusted minimum across historical procedures
is used.


\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/registered-reconstruction-fsc.pdf}
\caption{All twelve method/stack comparisons against original and pilot-registered
references; dotted lines mark FSC 0.5 and 0.143. G/V/N use supplied poses,
whereas RELION estimates poses. Registration is selected using the old pilot
only. Agreement includes preprocessing, interpolation and frame dependence;
censored crossings are not measured resolutions. On 10076 the Class A reference
is not truth for the heterogeneous consensus.}\label{fig:registeredfsc}
\end{figure*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/cubic-design-comparison.pdf}
\caption{All five cubic designs on the selected 10049 region. Left: minimum
conditional simulated sign power across three declared poses, retaining both
reference frames. Right: observed intervals under separately reported raw and
centered calibration; all contain zero. Each procedure retains the stated
$.05/12$ total error allocation under unverified model premises; the plot is
not an experimental coverage claim or an unadjusted selection rule across
procedures. The registered approximate reference is not biological truth.}
\label{fig:cubiccomparison}
\end{figure*}
